scenes.tts: The first film followed matter into sugar and wood. Now ask how fast that building can go. If light powers sugar-building, why can brighter light stop helping? Place the same plant inside a clear chamber. Its light dial starts low. A sugar meter waits beside it. We will change one condition at a time.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's colour map exactly: gold light energy, teal carbon dioxide, blue water, green sugar, and brown wood. Carry the same plant into a chamber that fills most of the frame. Add three large dials labelled LIGHT, CARBON DIOXIDE and TEMPERATURE, plus a green sugar-rate meter.
scenes.narration: The first film followed matter into sugar and wood. Now ask how fast that building can go. If light powers sugar-building, why can brighter light stop helping? Place the same plant inside a clear chamber. Its light dial starts low. A sugar meter waits beside it. We will change one condition at a time.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the moving chamber: 'Why More Light Stops Helping'. Keep blue water rising and a gold light beam shimmering.

scenes.tts: A rate tells how fast something happens. Here it tracks sugar made over time. Turn the light dial upward from dim. The gold beam brightens, and the green meter climbs. More light helps because light is holding the process back under these starting conditions.
scenes.visual: Turn the gold LIGHT dial slowly. Increase the gold beam width and raise the green meter together. Grow a large graph from the meter: light along the bottom, photosynthesis rate upward. Label this chamber curve 'schematic'. Keep the other two dials fixed and visibly locked.
scenes.narration: A rate tells how fast something happens. Here it tracks sugar made over time. Turn the light dial upward from dim. The gold beam brightens, and the green meter climbs. More light helps because light is holding the process back under these starting conditions.

scenes.tts: Keep turning the light dial. The curve still rises, but each equal turn adds less. Soon it bends toward a level stretch. The beam brightens again while the sugar meter barely moves. Light is plentiful now, so more light is no longer the main help.
scenes.visual: Extend the labelled schematic curve toward a plateau. Move a bright marker along it in equal horizontal steps while the vertical steps shrink. Keep the plant and dials visible. Brighten the gold beam once more while the green meter rises only slightly.
scenes.narration: Keep turning the light dial. The curve still rises, but each equal turn adds less. Soon it bends toward a level stretch. The beam brightens again while the sugar meter barely moves. Light is plentiful now, so more light is no longer the main help.

scenes.tts: Predict before the next turn. If the light is already bright, will doubling it double the photosynthesis rate? Watch the curve and choose.
scenes.visual: Place the marker near the plateau. Show a large gold arrow from BRIGHT to TWICE AS BRIGHT. Put two choices beside the graph: 'rate doubles' and 'rate changes little'. Keep the marker pulsing without moving.
scenes.narration: Predict before the next turn. If the light is already bright, will doubling it double the photosynthesis rate? Watch the curve and choose.

scenes.visual: Hold the question and both choices. Keep the plant leaves swaying and the gold beam shimmering. Do not mark an answer.

scenes.tts: Here the rate changes little. Something else is now the tighter limit. A limiting condition holds a process back. When one condition becomes plentiful, a different one may matter more. The level curve reveals a limit, but it does not name that limit by itself.
scenes.visual: Turn the light dial through the doubled step. Move the curve marker mostly sideways with only a tiny rise. Fade a gold LIMIT tag from the light dial. Then place neutral question marks over the teal carbon-dioxide dial, the temperature dial and the leaf itself. Do not select any one.
scenes.narration: Here the rate changes little. Something else is now the tighter limit. A limiting condition holds a process back. When one condition becomes plentiful, a different one may matter more. The level curve reveals a limit, but it does not name that limit by itself.

scenes.tts: Carbon dioxide can limit the rate. Raising it may help after light stops helping. Temperature also changes the rate. Warming can speed the process up to a point. Too much heat slows it down. These conditions interact, so the important limit can change.
scenes.visual: Keep bright light locked. Turn the teal CARBON DIOXIDE dial and let the green meter rise, with a note 'may rise'. Reset it. Then sweep the TEMPERATURE dial from cold to warm to hot while a separate schematic rate curve rises and falls. Mark both demonstrations 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Carbon dioxide can limit the rate. Raising it may help after light stops helping. Temperature also changes the rate. Warming can speed the process up to a point. Too much heat slows it down. These conditions interact, so the important limit can change.

scenes.tts: Light powers sugar-building from carbon dioxide and water; conditions limit its speed. This rule keeps two questions together. The first asks what supplies energy and matter. The second asks what controls the rate under these conditions. Answering one does not answer the other.
scenes.visual: Bring the exact rule across the top. Under it, split the chamber into two linked panels. The left carries gold energy plus teal and blue matter into green sugar. The right carries the three dials into one rate gauge. Animate a thin connector between the panels.
scenes.narration: Light powers sugar-building from carbon dioxide and water; conditions limit its speed. This rule keeps two questions together. The first asks what supplies energy and matter. The second asks what controls the rate under these conditions. Answering one does not answer the other.

scenes.tts: Real blueberry leaves show the same useful shape. At low light, added light raised carbon dioxide uptake strongly. At high light, much more added light changed uptake only a little. Those measurements show where light stopped being the main limit. They do not identify the next limit.
scenes.visual: Replace the schematic curve with a plot computed from the blueberry table values from 25 to 1,500 light units; leave out the zero-light point, which the lesson discusses. Relabel the vertical axis 'carbon dioxide taken in (net)'. Put the numeric light and uptake values on screen but do not speak them. Label the points 'measured, approximate values read from Figure 4'. Trace the steep low-light section, then the nearly level high-light section.
scenes.narration: Real blueberry leaves show the same useful shape. At low light, added light raised carbon dioxide uptake strongly. At high light, much more added light changed uptake only a little. Those measurements show where light stopped being the main limit. They do not identify the next limit.

scenes.tts: Use a curve as a clue, not a slogan. A steep rise says the changed condition mattered strongly. A level stretch says more of it helped little. Then test another condition while holding the others steady. That is how a simple chamber becomes a fair investigation. When more light stops helping, something else is holding the rate back.
scenes.visual: Return to the full chamber. Highlight the steep part, then the plateau. Lock two dials and turn the third. Swap which dial is free, resetting the rate meter before each test. End with the plant, all three dials and the measured curve visible together.
scenes.narration: Use a curve as a clue, not a slogan. A steep rise says the changed condition mattered strongly. A level stretch says more of it helped little. Then test another condition while holding the others steady. That is how a simple chamber becomes a fair investigation. When more light stops helping, something else is holding the rate back.

scenes.visual: One-line end card only: 'When more light stops helping, something else is holding the rate back.' No title, website, subtitle or smaller line. Keep a faint green curve marker moving behind the single line.
